findings.issue_text: Feed article HTML is stored and rendered without sanitization, allowing malicious feeds to persist scripts or event handlers and cause stored XSS
Embed URLs are interpolated unescaped into a single-quoted href in raw HTML, so quotes can inject attributes or markup and cause stored XSS
The host allowlist checks only the initial URL and does not revalidate redirect destinations, enabling SSRF to internal services through an approved host's redirect endpoint
The feed poller assumes every item has content, so RSS items containing only description cause nil.scrub to abort the entire polling run
absolutize_urls leaves document-relative links unresolved against the article URL, causing them to resolve against the Discourse host
absolutize_urls incorrectly rewrites protocol-relative URLs under the article host
Missing-embed requests enqueue jobs before throttling, allowing forged Referer headers and distinct URLs to grow the job queue without bound
Embed message origins are validated with substring matching, allowing similar but unrelated origins to manipulate iframe height

goldens.comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

per_golden_matches.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the same security vulnerability as the golden comment. Both point out that the origin validation using substring/indexOf matching is insufficient and can be bypassed by similar but unrelated origins. The golden comment gives a specific example (evil-discourseUrl.com), while the candidate describes the same problem more generally as 'similar but unrelated origins' being able to manipulate the iframe. They are describing the exact same security flaw.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Feed article HTML is stored and rendered without sanitization, allowing malicious feeds to persist scripts or event handlers and cause stored XSS

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, in app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb, the feed content is processed with `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` and passed to `TopicEmbed.import`. In TopicEmbed.import, the content is stored with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. In app/models/post.rb, when cook_method is :raw_html, the cook method returns `raw` directly without any sanitization: `return raw if cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. This means RSS/Atom feed content is rendered as raw HTML without sanitization. Additionally, in import_remote, ruby-readability extracts content with limited tag filtering but the content still goes through the same raw_html path. The view in best.html.erb uses `raw post.cooked` which outputs the unsanitized HTML directly. This is a real stored XSS vulnerability - malicious feed content with scripts or event handlers would be stored and rendered to users.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The host allowlist checks only the initial URL and does not revalidate redirect destinations, enabling SSRF to internal services through an approved host's redirect endpoint

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, the TopicRetriever class checks if the embed URL's host matches the embeddable_host setting in the invalid_host? method. However, when fetch_http is called, it delegates to TopicEmbed.import_remote which uses open(url).read via ruby-readability. The open-uri library in Ruby follows HTTP redirects by default. If an attacker controls a page on the allowed host that redirects to an internal service (e.g., http://allowed-host.com/redirect?to=http://169.254.169.254/metadata), the initial host check would pass, but the actual HTTP request would follow the redirect to the internal service. This is a valid SSRF vulnerability because the host validation only happens on the initial URL, not on redirect destinations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: absolutize_urls leaves document-relative links unresolved against the article URL, causing them to resolve against the Discourse host

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the absolutize_urls method in topic_embed.rb, it only handles URLs that start with '/'. The code checks `if href.present? && href.start_with?('/')` for links and `if src.present? && src.start_with?('/')` for images. This means document-relative links (like 'hello' without a leading slash, or '../page') would not be converted to absolute URLs. However, examining the test case in the spec, the content uses `<a href='/hello'>` which starts with '/', so it would be handled. The finding claims document-relative links are unresolved, which is technically true - links like 'relative/path' (without leading slash) would not be absolutized. This is a real limitation in the code that could cause broken links when RSS content contains document-relative URLs (without leading slash). The code only handles root-relative URLs (starting with /).

adjudication_records.issue_text: absolutize_urls incorrectly rewrites protocol-relative URLs under the article host

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the absolutize_urls method in app/models/topic_embed.rb, it checks if href/src start_with?('/') before rewriting. Protocol-relative URLs like '//example.com/image.jpg' do start with '/', so they would be incorrectly rewritten to 'http://eviltrout.com//example.com/image.jpg'. The code does `a['href'] = "#{prefix}/#{href.sub(/^\/+/, '')}"` which strips leading slashes, but this would turn '//cdn.example.com/img.jpg' into 'http://eviltrout.com/cdn.example.com/img.jpg' - still incorrect. This is a real bug where protocol-relative URLs would be corrupted.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Missing-embed requests enqueue jobs before throttling, allowing forged Referer headers and distinct URLs to grow the job queue without bound

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the EmbedController#best method, when no topic_id is found, it calls Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...) before any throttling occurs. The throttling logic is in TopicRetriever#retrieved_recently? which uses Redis setnx with a 60-second expiry, but this happens INSIDE the job execution, not before enqueueing. The ensure_embeddable method does check the referer against embeddable_host, but an attacker could forge the Referer header to match the configured embeddable_host while using many different embed_url values. Each unique embed_url would enqueue a new job. The throttling in TopicRetriever is per-URL (retrieved_key = 'retrieved:#{@embed_url}'), so different URLs bypass each other's throttles. This means an attacker with a valid Referer header could flood the job queue with requests for many different URLs.
